paragraphs.text: Raw pu’er from Yunnan, made in 1980 and kept as loose leaf. At forty-six years it sits well past any line the trade draws for [aged](sheng:ageing): some count from ten years, many wait for twenty or more.

[Sheng](sheng:identity) is never given the quick fermentation of shou, so [it changes slowly in storage](sheng:aging), and the years it has been kept become part of its history. It was never pressed: a tight, large cake changes slowly, while [loose or small tea](sheng:pressing) changes sooner.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
